questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass 1.5 kg moves along the floor of a hall with a speed of $5\ ms^{-1}$. It strikes an uncompressed spring and compresses it till the block becomes motionless. If the force constant of the spring is 10000 Nm^{-1}$ and the spring is compressed by 5cm, calculate the effective force of kinetic friction.$
questions.solution:
Initial kinetic energy of the block is $K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

Final kinetic energy of the block is $K_f = 0$.

Work done by the spring force is $W_s = -\dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

Work done by the kinetic friction is $W_f = -f_k x$.

Using the work-energy theorem, $W_s + W_f = K_f - K_i$.

$-\dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 - f_k x = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

$f_k x = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

Substituting the given values: $m = 1.5$ kg, $v = 5$ m/s, $k = 10000$ N/m, $x = 0.05$ m.

$f_k (0.05) = \dfrac{1}{2}(1.5)(5)^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(10000)(0.05)^2$

$f_k (0.05) = 18.75 - 12.5$

$f_k (0.05) = 6.25$

$f_k = \dfrac{6.25}{0.05} = 125$ N

Answer: $125$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball falls under gravity from a height of 10m with an initial downward velocity $u$. It loses three-fifths (or 60%) of its energy in collision and then rises back to 5m. The initial velocity $u$ is ($g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the ball be $m$

Initial total energy of the ball at height $h_1 = 10$ is $E_i = mgh_1 + \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$

$E_i = m(10)(10) + 0.5mu^2 = 100m + 0.5mu^2$

The ball loses $60\%$ of its energy upon collision, so the remaining energy is $0.4E_i$

The ball rises to a height $h_2 = 5$, so the final energy at the highest point is $E_f = mgh_2 = m(10)(5) = 50m$

Equating the remaining energy to the final energy gives $0.4(100m + 0.5mu^2) = 50m$

$40m + 0.2mu^2 = 50m$

$0.2u^2 = 10$

$u^2 = 50$

$u = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07 ms^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A motor cyclist starts from the top of an inclined plane of height h to go around a globe of death trap of radius r. The ratio of minimum height 'h' of the inclined plane to the radius 'r' of the death globe in order to go around the death globe successfully is
questions.solution:
By conservation of mechanical energy, the velocity of the motorcyclist at the bottom of the inclined plane is given by

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

$v = \sqrt{2gh}$

To successfully complete the vertical circular loop (globe of death) of radius $r$, the minimum velocity required at the lowest point is

$v \ge \sqrt{5gr}$

For the minimum height $h$, we equate the velocities:

$\sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{5gr}$

$2gh = 5gr$

$\dfrac{h}{r} = \dfrac{5}{2}$

The ratio of the minimum height to the radius is $5:2$.

Answer: $5:2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from a height of 2 m on the top of the spring of length 0.6 m , fixed vertically on the horizontal table. If the spring is depressed by a distance of 10 cm , then what will be the spring constant of the spring? $g=10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$
questions.solution:
Total height fallen: $h = (2 - 0.6) + 0.1 = 1.5$ m

By energy conservation:

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$

$0.5 \times 10 \times 1.5 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times k \times (0.1)^2$

$7.5 = 0.005k$

$k = 1500 \ Nm^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wind mill converts a fixed fraction of the wind energy intercepted by its blades into electrical energy. The electrical power output P is related to the velocity of wind v as
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy $K$ of a mass $m$ of air moving with velocity $v$ is given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

The mass $m$ of air passing through an area $A$ in time $t$ is $m = \rho A v t$, where $\rho$ is the density of air.

The power $P$ is the rate of change of energy, $P = \dfrac{K}{t} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{m}{t} \right) v^2$.

Substituting the expression for mass flow rate $\dfrac{m}{t} = \rho A v$, we get $P = \dfrac{1}{2} (\rho A v) v^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho A v^3$.

Since the windmill converts a fixed fraction of this energy, the electrical power output $P$ is directly proportional to $v^3$.

Answer: $v^3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vertical spring of spring constant $24 \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ is fixed on a table. A ball of mass 0.5 kg at a height 2 m above the free upper end of the spring falls vertically on the spring so that the spring is compressed by a distance of 50 cm. The net work done in the process is:
questions.solution:
The ball falls from a height $h = 2$ m above the spring and compresses the spring by $x = 0.5$ m. The total vertical displacement of the ball is $H = h + x = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5$ m.

The work done by gravity on the ball is $W_{g} = mgH = 0.5 \times 9.8 \times 2.5 = 12.25$ J. Using $g = 10$ m/s^{2}$ for standard approximation in such problems, $W_{g} = 0.5 \times 10 \times 2.5 = 12.5$ J.

The work done by the spring force is $W_{s} = -$\dfrac{1}{2}$ kx^{2} = -$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 24 \times (0.5)^{2} = -12 \times 0.25 = -3$ J.

The net work done on the ball during the process is the sum of the work done by gravity and the work done by the spring force: $W_{net} = W_{g} + W_{s} = 12.5 - 3 = 9.5$ J.

Answer: 9.5 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object of mass $3\text{ kg}$ moves due to an applied constant force such that its position along X axis is given by $x = \dfrac{t^{\mathrm{2}}}{3}$ where $x$ is in meters and $t$ in seconds. The work done in 1 second is
questions.solution:
$x = \dfrac{t^2}{3} \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{2t}{3}$

At $t = 0$: $v_i = 0$, at $t = 1$ s: $v_f = \dfrac{2}{3}$ m/s

By work-energy theorem:

$W = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mv_i^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 - 0 = \dfrac{3}{2} \times \dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An electric motor raises a mass of $1.5 \mathrm{ kg}$, a distance of $1.128 \mathrm{ m}$ in time of $4.79 \mathrm{ s}$. Calculate the power to an appropriate significant figures.
(take $g=9.81 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The power $P$ is defined as the rate of doing work, which is given by $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{mgh}{t}$.

Given values are $m = 1.5 \text{ kg}$, $g = 9.81 \text{ ms}^{-2}$, $h = 1.128 \text{ m}$, and $t = 4.79 \text{ s}$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$P = \dfrac{1.5 \times 9.81 \times 1.128}{4.79}$

$P = \dfrac{16.59732}{4.79} \approx 3.465$ W.

The given values have the following significant figures: $1.5$ (2 sig figs), $1.128$ (4 sig figs), $4.79$ (3 sig figs). The result should be reported to the least number of significant figures present in the data, which is 2.

Rounding $3.465$ to two significant figures gives $3.5$ W.

Answer: 3.5 W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A scooter moves with a speed of $7 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$, on a straight road and is stopped by applying the brakes. Before stopping, the scooter travels $10 \mathrm{ m}$. If the weight of the scooter is $\mathrm{W}$, then the total resistance to the motion of the scooter will be
questions.solution:
Given initial speed $u = 7 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$, final speed $v = 0$, and distance $s = 10 \mathrm{ m}$.

Using the equation of motion $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, we have $0 = 7^2 + 2a(10)$.

$0 = 49 + 20a \Rightarrow a = -\dfrac{49}{20} \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$.

The retarding force $F$ is given by Newton's second law $F = ma = \dfrac{W}{g} a$.

Substituting the values, $F = \dfrac{W}{9.8} \times \left( -\dfrac{49}{20} \right).

Since 9.8 = \dfrac{98}{10} = \dfrac{49}{5}, we have $ F = $\dfrac{W}{49/5} \times \left( -\dfrac{49}{20} \right) =$ W $\times \dfrac{5}{49} \times \left( -\dfrac{49}{20} \right) = -\dfrac{5}{20}$ W = -$\dfrac{1}{4}$ W$.

The magnitude of the resistance force is \dfrac{1}{4}$ W$.

Answer: \dfrac{1}{4}$ W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When water falls from a height of $80 \mathrm{ m}$ at the rate of $20 \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$ to operate a turbine the losses due to frictional force are $20 \%$ of input energy. How much power is generated by the turbine?
questions.solution:
The potential energy of the water falling per unit time is the input power, given by $P_{in} = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = \left(\dfrac{m}{t}\right)gh$.

Given $\dfrac{m}{t} = 20 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$, $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $h = 80 \text{ m}$, we have $P_{in} = 20 \times 10 \times 80 = 16000 \text{ W} = 16 \text{ kW}$.

The losses due to frictional force are $20 \%$ of the input energy, so the efficiency of the turbine is $100 \% - 20 \% = 80 \%$.

The power generated by the turbine is $P_{out} = 80 \% \text{ of } P_{in} = 0.8 \times 16 \text{ kW} = 12.8 \text{ kW}$.

Answer: 12.8 KW

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The power of a gun which fires 120 bullet per minute with a velocity $120 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ is : (given the mass of each bullet is $100 \mathrm{ g}$)
questions.solution:
The number of bullets fired per second is $n = \dfrac{120}{60} = 2$ bullets per second.

The mass of each bullet is $m = 100 \text{ g} = 0.1 \text{ kg}$.

The velocity of each bullet is $v = 120 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

The kinetic energy of one bullet is $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.1 \times (120)^2 = 0.05 \times 14400 = 720 \text{ J}$.

The power of the gun is the total kinetic energy delivered per second, which is $P = n \times K = 2 \times 720 = 1440 \text{ W}$.

Converting to kilowatts, $P = \dfrac{1440}{1000} \text{ kW} = 1.44 \text{ kW}$.

Answer: 1.44 kW

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If reaction is $\mathrm{R}$ and coefficient of friction is $\mu$, what is work done against friction in moving a body by distance $\mathrm{d}$ ?
questions.solution:
The force of kinetic friction $f_k$ acting on a body is given by the product of the coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu$ and the normal reaction force $R$.

$f_k = \mu R$

The work done $W$ against friction when moving a body by a distance $d$ is defined as the product of the frictional force and the displacement, since the frictional force acts in the direction opposite to the displacement.

$W = f_k \times d$

Substituting the expression for $f_k$ into the work formula:

$W = (\mu R) \times d = \mu Rd$

Answer: $\mu \mathrm{Rd}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long spring, when stretched by a distance $x$, has potential energy $U$. On increasing the stretching to $n x$, the potential energy of the spring will be
questions.solution:
The potential energy $U$ stored in a spring stretched by a distance $x$ is given by the formula $U = \dfrac{1}{2} k x^{2}$, where $k$ is the spring constant.

When the stretching is increased to $n x$, the new potential energy $U'$ is given by $U' = \dfrac{1}{2} k (n x)^{2}$.

Expanding the expression, we get $U' = \dfrac{1}{2} k n^{2} x^{2}$.

Substituting the original potential energy $U = \dfrac{1}{2} k x^{2}$ into the expression for $U'$, we obtain $U' = n^{2} (\dfrac{1}{2} k x^{2}) = n^{2} U$.

Answer: $n^2 U$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is projected at an angle $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ with horizontal having kinetic energy $K$. The kinetic energy of the particle at highest point is.
questions.solution:
Let the initial velocity of the particle be $u$. The initial kinetic energy is given by $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$.

At the highest point of the trajectory, the vertical component of the velocity becomes zero, while the horizontal component remains constant. The horizontal component of the velocity is $v_x = u \cos \theta$, where $\theta = 30^{{}^{\circ}}$.

The kinetic energy at the highest point $K'$ is given by $K' = \dfrac{1}{2}m(v_x)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}m(u \cos 30^{{}^{\circ}})^2$.

Substituting $\cos 30^{{}^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, we get $K' = \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2 \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2$.

Since $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$, we have $K' = K \times \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}K$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{4} K$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One end of the string of length $l$ is connected to a particle of mass $m$ and the other end is connected to a small peg on a smooth horizontal table. If the particle moves in circle with speed $v$, the net force on the particle (directed towards centre) will be (T$ represents the tension in the string)$
questions.solution:
The particle moves in a circle on a smooth horizontal table. Vertical forces (gravity and normal reaction) balance each other.

In the horizontal plane, the only force acting towards the centre is the tension $T$ in the string.

This tension provides the centripetal force: $T = \dfrac{mv^2}{l}$

Net force directed towards centre $= T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is moving in a horizontal circle of radius $r$ under a centripetal force given by $\left(\dfrac{-K}{r^2}\right)$, where $K$ is a constant. Then
options: the total energy of the particle is $\left(\dfrac{-K}{2 r}\right)$
the kinetic energy of the particle is $\left(\dfrac{K}{r}\right)$
the potential energy of the particle is $\left(\dfrac{K}{2 r}\right)$
the kinetic energy of the particle is $\left(\dfrac{-K}{r}\right)$
questions.solution:
The centripetal force acting on the particle is given by $F = \dfrac{-K}{r^2}$. The magnitude of the centripetal force is $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{K}{r^2}$.

From this, the kinetic energy $K.E.$ is calculated as $K.E. = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{K}{r} \right) = \dfrac{K}{2r}$.

The potential energy $U$ is defined by $F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr}$. Integrating the force $F = -\dfrac{K}{r^2}$ with respect to $r$, we get $U = \int \dfrac{K}{r^2} dr = -\dfrac{K}{r}$.

The total energy $E$ is the sum of kinetic energy and potential energy: $E = K.E. + U = \dfrac{K}{2r} - \dfrac{K}{r} = -\dfrac{K}{2r}$.

Comparing this with the given options, the total energy of the particle is $-\dfrac{K}{2r}$.

Answer: the total energy of the particle is $\left(\dfrac{-K}{2 r}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For motion under central forces, which quantity will be conserved ?
questions.solution:
A central force is a force that is directed along the line joining the source of the force and the particle, and its magnitude depends only on the distance $r$ from the source. Such a force can be expressed as $\vec{F} = f(r)\hat{r}$.

Since the force is purely radial, the torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = \vec{r} \times f(r)\hat{r} = 0$. Consequently, the angular momentum $\vec{L}$ is conserved.

Furthermore, a central force is a conservative force because it is a function of position only and its curl is zero. For any conservative force field, the total mechanical energy $E = K + U$ is conserved, where $K$ is the kinetic energy and $U$ is the potential energy.

Among the given options, mechanical energy is the quantity that is conserved in motion under central forces.

Answer: Mechanical energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a body moves in a circular path, no work is done by the force since
options: force and displacement are perpendicular to each other
the force is always away from the centre
questions.solution:
The work done by a force in moving a body is W=\underline{F} $\cdot \mathbf{S}$ where, $s$ is the displacement vector.
In circular path, the force is centripetal, thus always acting towards the centre along the radial direction.
However, the displacement is always along tangent to the circle at the instantaneous position of object.
Hence, $\theta=90^{{}^{\circ}}$
Thus, $\quad W=\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{s}=F s \cos 90^{{}^{\circ}}=0$

In a circular path, the centripetal force acts towards the centre of circle and the displacement is along the tangent to the circle. Hence, $\theta=90^{{}^{\circ}}\therefore$ Work done $W=\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{s}=F s \cos \theta$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One coolie takes $1\mathrm\min$ to raise a suitcase through a height of $2 \mathrm{ m}$ but the second coolie takes $30 \mathrm{ s}$ to raise the same suitcase to the same height. The powers of two coolies are in the ratio.
questions.solution:
Here, work done $=m g h$
As, $m$ and $h$ is same, so work done will be same in both cases.
Power, $P=\frac{\text{ Work done }(W)}{\text{ Time taken }(t)}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}=\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}=\frac{30}{60}=\frac{1}{2}$ or $1: 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $120 \mathrm{ J}$ of work is done in $2 \mathrm{ min}$ by a water pump, then the power of the pump is
questions.solution:
Given, work done, $W=120 \mathrm{ J}$
Time, $t=2 \mathrm{ min}=2 \times 60=120 \mathrm{ s}\therefore$ Power $=\frac{\text{ Work done }}{\text{ Time }}=\frac{W}{t}=\frac{120}{120}=1 \mathrm{ W}$
